question: What was his confessional allegiance?
proposition: Ibn Turka's confessional position is ambiguous and best called Shiʿi-Sunnism or imamophilism, a defining feature of 9th/15th-century religiosity, neither Corbin's Shiʿism nor Lewisohn's Sunni orthodoxy.
reasoning: Grounds: his heavy emphasis on the Imams as sources of occult knowledge (pdf p.86); impeccable Shafiʿi credentials, though Shafiʿism is an unreliable marker of Sunnism (p.90); a Sunni-tradition Sharh al-Nahj and a Sunni salaf passage in the Mafahis (pp.91-92); a Shiʿi-looking alteration of Ibn al-Farid's Tāʾiyya (p.92).
MK's objection to Corbin is that his openly-Shiʿi verdict ignores the age's confessional ambiguity, and to Lewisohn that the Sunni Sufi reading takes the apologies at face value (p.25).

Pages 93 onward, where MK's discussion of this point continues, were not read for this task; the dissertation may qualify the reading there. MK reads the Mafahis salaf passage as a concession to the unintelligent (p.92 n.150), which is an interpretation, not a fact of the text.
MK is a partisan reporter. Confidence records how fully the pages of MK's dissertation let us reconstruct this position and its grounds, not whether it is true.
